New Late Cretaceous paleomagnetic results from the Lhasa
terrane and their implications for the suturing of India and
Eurasia and the closure of the Neo-Tethys Ocean

2 Key Laboratory of Paleomagnetism and Tectonic Reconstruction, Ministry of Land and Resources, Beijing 100081, China
3 College of Resources, Environment and Tourism, Capital Normal University, Beijing 100048, China

### page_10
Suturing process of India and Eurasia and closure of the Neo-Tethys Ocean
the Lhasa terrane was oriented around 317°
during the Cretaceous (Fig. 6B).
Subduction Direction of the Neo-Tethys Ocean during the Late Cretaceous
The subduction of the Neo-Tethys oce-
anic lithosphere beneath Eurasia not only induced the continuous mountain building of
an ∼2500-km-long, Andean-type Gangdese
orogenic belt along the subduction zone, but it
also applied continuous stress to southern Eur- asia, inducing progressive crustal shortening and deformation of the southeastern part of the
Lhasa terrane (Yin and Harrison, 2000; Kapp
et al., 2007; Leier et al., 2007). The subduction
of the Neo-Tethys Ocean beneath Eurasia along a stabilized direction and the parallel collision
of India and Eurasia could have applied a stable
stress to the Lhasa terrane, forming a series of
straight fold axes in the Cretaceous strata of the
Lhasa terrane, which were approximately per-
pendicular to the subduction direction. Oppo-
sitely, changes in the subduction direction of the
Neo-Tethys Ocean and diachronous collision of
India and Eurasia could have induced a pro- gressive change in the compressional direction,
forming a curved tectonic line imparting the
fold axes of the Cretaceous strata of the Lhasa terrane (Fig. 7). Thus, the process of suturing
of the Neo-Tethys Ocean can be precisely con-
strained according to the form of the tectonic
line represented by the original fold axes of the
Cretaceous strata within the Lhasa terrane.
The Cretaceous paleomagnetic data sets
from different parts of the Lhasa terrane show significant dispersion of declination, which
was related to the different rotational defor-
mation and/or composite folding of sampled
strata. In order to reveal the dominant mecha-
nism for the dispersion of declination, the
plunge direction and dip of composite fold axes
in each section were calculated to correct the
Cretaceous paleomagnetic data sets (Table 4). The corrections showed that the observed dec- linations are indistinguishable from the cor- rected declinations (Fig. 8A), indicating that the dispersion of declination was not induced
by the composite folding. The Cretaceous
paleopoles of Europe (Torsvik et al., 2012)
were selected as reference poles to constrain the rotational characteristics of sections, and
they show that the Lhasa terrane experienced
different rotation, with accumulated rotational
degrees in a wide range of −55.2° ± 6.5° to
30.9° ± 7.3° (where the positive and negative
values represent clockwise and counterclock-
wise rotation, respectively). The correlation
of Sr–S (where Sr and S are the strike of the
reference regional tectonic line and the strike

Figure 8. (A) Observed and tilt-corrected
A
declination by plunge direction and dip of
composite fold axis of each section. Method 1:
First rotated the fold axis back to horizontal
and then corrected the data from the residual
bedding dip. Method 2: First rotated the bed-
ding strikes in a direction normal to the fold
axis direction and then corrected the data
from the axis dip. (B) Best-fit linear regression
for Sr (strike of reference regional tectonic
lines)–S (strike of fold axis) and the accumu-
lated rotational degree (ARD). (C) Almost-
parallel arrangement of the margins of the
Lhasa terrane (LT) and Tethyan Himalaya
(TH), and the straight fold axes of the Creta-
ceous strata in the southern part of the Lhasa
B
terrane indicate that the subduction direction
of the Neo-Tethys Ocean and the movement of
the Tethyan Himalaya were consistently main-
tained in the stabilized direction of 62.5° ± 8.5°
prior to the collision of India and Eurasia. The
overlap of the northern margin of the central
Tethyan Himalaya with the southern margin
of the central Lhasa terrane during 59.0–
56.0 Ma indicates that the Tethyan Himalaya
quasi-parallelly collided with the Lhasa ter-
rane at that time, which quasi-synchronously
closed the Neo-Tethys Ocean.
CONCLUSIONS
The Cretaceous paleomagnetic data sets
C
from the Lhasa terrane and the Paleocene
to Eocene paleomagnetic data sets from the
Tethyan Himalaya indicate that the southern
margin of the Lhasa terrane in the longitude
range of 80.6°E to 91.0°E was originally ori-
ented ∼317° prior to the collision of India
and Eurasia, and the northern margin of the
Tethyan Himalaya in the longitude range of
85.3°E to 89.2°E was oriented at ∼326° dur-
ing 62.0–59.2 Ma. The margins of the Lhasa
terrane and Tethyan Himalaya were almost
parallel with the tectonic line (oriented
332.5° ± 8.5°) recorded by the original fold
axes of Cretaceous strata in the southern part
of the Lhasa terrane, indicating that the sub-
duction direction of Neo-Tethys oceanic litho-
sphere beneath Eurasia and the northeastward
movement of the Tethyan Himalaya were con-
sistently maintained in a stabilized direction
et al., 2021). During 59.0–56.0 Ma, the north- lung-Zangbo suture zone. This conclusion is of 62.5° ± 8.5° prior to the collision of the
